MuJoCo · PPO → MJX/GPU · training log · updated 2026·08·24

update · 2026·09·03 · hardware thread

Three follow-ups, one correction, one honest negative. Correction first: the policy on the robot is loco_v26lag_s128 (the board's stat says so), trained WITH the 2–12 Hz act-lag pole and 0.5–1° backlash — last night's sim comparisons used the v22fix student by mistake. Redone with the right policy: still dead still in sim (upy RMS 0.0009 vs 0.05–0.13 on the robot). (1) Fine sweep. At 0.25° steps the left hip roll shows a textbook backlash step: no torso response until +3.25°, then a jump to 1.3° that holds through the reversal all the way down to +1.25° — 2° of hysteresis, ~3° from home to engagement. Right hip roll stays unresolved (≤0.4° response). Knees: the left tracks smoothly (0.27° hysteresis); the right at +3.5° tipped the whole robot 7° (guard fired, homed cleanly) — the right leg carries the weight, third time it shows. (2) Play in the twin. walker_env gained a FREE-TRAVEL model (play_deg/play_joints: a massless shaft tracks the command at the no-load speed, the link is driven only outside ±play/2 and floats undamped inside), exposed as sil_twin --play-deg --play-joints. Result: 3° or 6° on the hip rolls or on all ten joints, with or without 2 Hz lag, and the flashed policy still stands dead still (upy RMS ≤ 0.002). So static mechanical hysteresis, on its own, is not the mechanism — the hardware loop is being excited by something the twin lacks. Remaining candidates, in the order I'd test them: the asymmetric right-foot stance (sim stands symmetric), foot/mat compliance, the complementary-filter up-vector (sim's is exact), and dq/gyro noise. (3) Firmware: the reset verdict now means moved. homeAll returns HOME_PENDING (8) after the broadcast write; cli::homeVerify, on the housekeeping loop, reads all ten joints back once the slew deadline passes (worst move ÷ speed + 0.7 s) and stores DISARMED_HOME only when every joint is within 12 ticks of its zero, else HOME_NOT_REACHED (9) with the offenders named on the tether. Flashed 09:01, verified over the link: PENDING at 0.45 s, DISARMED_HOME at 0.90 s, UART "home readback: all 10 joints at their zeros". Both probes wait out PENDING; tools/home_verify.py watches the sequence. One more bench note: the servos had lost torque overnight (home left them holding at 23:00; at 08:50 a goal write was refused "torque is OFF"; pack 12.0 V, no faults, no reboot, cause unknown) — check torque before any bench run. Data: hw_sessions/2026-09-03/.

Later: Tom's yaw suspicion, a wrong inference, and the eye test that caught it. Tom: the hip yaw joints likely have the most play — "the entire leg is controlled by the tiny servo axis" — and the mat is not a factor since the feet have no traction pads. Yaw does not tilt the torso and the encoders sit on the shaft side of the slop, so tools/yaw_probe.py yaws the hips in 2° steps and reads the pelvis yaw off the gyro (projected on the measured gravity axis, bias-corrected per step, integrated over each slow move; the board streams imu raw at ~11 Hz). Rigid-sim reference (sim/joint_yaw_sim.py): both hips the same way → pelvis 0.78°/°, one hip 0.45°/°, opposite signs ~0. The robot did the reverse — same-sign commands cancelled, opposite-sign turned the pelvis 2.0°/1.65°, right-only went the other way from left-only — and I read that as one hip yaw mirrored against the model, pointing at R_hip_yaw, and asked for an eye check before touching the calibration. The eye check refuted it. Right hip +10°: the right toe swung to the robot's left (inward) — the model's direction. Left hip +10°: the left foot stayed planted and the rest of the robot swung right, so the left toe points outward — also the robot's left in body terms, also the model's direction. Nothing is mirrored; both as-built yaw signs are right. What the gyro had measured: the weight was on the left foot this morning (it was on the right last night — the stance asymmetry flips between re-homings), so the right foot slides, and a right-yaw command mostly reacts back into the pelvis, which turns the other way inside the left yaw chain's slop while the left servo holds. Read correctly, that is a yaw-play measurement: the left yaw chain let the pelvis move ≥1.2° under reaction torque with its servo holding, and every yaw move stalled 10–12 ticks (~1°) short of its goal in both directions. So yaw play is ~1–2°, the same order as the 2–3° in roll, not dramatically larger. Two lessons, both already in the rules: a gyro-inferred sign is not a direction check, and never change cal dir on inferred evidence. Data: hw_sessions/2026-09-03/yaw2.csv, yaw3_opposite.csv, yawcheck_*.jpg, sim_ref/sim_yaw.txt.

update · 2026·09·02 · hardware thread · evening

The arm-and-fall is real, it is a ROLL limit cycle, and the sim cannot produce it — with any backlash. Tom: "when I arm the robot it begins a growing oscillation that eventually results in it falling over" and "a fair amount of play in the joints that might not be well modeled by the sim". Repeated from mira three times with cameras, beacon joint angles (the new 40 B pose frame) and obsdump all rolling (link/osc_probe.py: ARM|POSE zero-command stand with a tilt/swing guard → ESTOP + disarm; --home proved RESET SERVOS over the link live: verdict DISARMED_HOME, every joint within 0.014 rad of zero, torque holding). Run 1 stood 8 s; runs 2 and 3 fell 8.5 s and 18.8 s after arming, both sideways (upy → +0.50 / −0.82, roll rate 2–3.5 rad/s at the end). It is not a smooth exponential: bursts of ~1 Hz rocking (joint p-p 0.2–0.4 rad in a 1 s window) separated by quiet seconds, then one burst tips it; the torso stays inside ~10° until the last half second, so a tilt guard cannot save it and a limp robot mid-sway falls anyway. The sensors are not the story this time: reported joint velocity vs finite-differenced angle has slope 0.69 (a unit error would be 50×; the dq quantum is exactly 0.0767 rad/s = one 0.732 rpm LSB) and the gyro RMS matches the roll the up-vector shows. The same policy (loco_v22fix_e_s128), same zero command, in the SIL twin: upy RMS 0.0009 vs 0.05–0.13 on the robot, gyrox 0.005 vs 0.67 (144×), dq 0.02 vs 0.35–0.47. So the twin got plant knobs (sil_twin --backlash-deg --act-lag-hz) and a sweep ran: 0 / 0.7 / 3 / 6 / 10° backlash × 0 / 2 Hz lag — every point stands dead still (upy RMS ≤ 0.0024, roll p-p ≤ 0.04 rad). The sim's "backlash" is a deadzone on the PD error, i.e. a servo that ignores small commands; the robot's play is the joint moving FREELY under load inside the slop — passive hysteresis in the only lateral actuator (no ankle roll on this body), which a command deadzone does not model at all. That is the gap Tom pointed at, now with numbers. Also different: the two plants settle in different postures (sim leans upx +0.13 with ankles −0.10; hardware upx −0.08…+0.03 with ankles +0.04…+0.07, L/R hip pitch −0.09/+0.10). Next, in order: (1) measure the play — link/play_probe.py is the torque-off pose stream, Tom wiggles each joint, per-joint p-p in degrees falls out; (2) one stand on a hard floor instead of the mat, same probe, to split surface compliance from joint slop; (3) model what we measure as plant hysteresis (free travel), not a command deadzone, and re-run this sweep until the twin rocks like the robot does — only then re-rank the fleet on it. Media + CSVs: hw_sessions/2026-09-02/osc(1, 2, 3)_* and sim_ref/.

Later the same evening — the play, estimated without hands. Tom stepped away, so the "wiggle each joint" measurement became a machine one: tools/joint_sweep.py steps ONE joint ±4° in 0.5° increments from the home stand (bench move, 60 steps/s) while the other nine hold, logging servo position, load and IMU tilt; sim/joint_sweep_sim.py runs the identical sweep on the rigid plant; tools/joint_sweep_compare.py puts them side by side. Two things the sim saved me from misreading. (1) The STS3215 load register is useless for static stiffness: every joint reached every goal within 6 ticks with load never leaving its idle ±24–56 band — the geartrain carries static load with the motor idle. (2) A hip-roll sweep barely tilts the torso even in sim (0.7° per 4°), so a small roll response is not play. Hysteresis is. Sim traces retrace to 0.1°; on the robot L hip roll held the torso 1.2° tilted through ~3° of command reversal before letting go, R hip pitch ~1°, L ankle ~0.5°, the rest under 0.3° (R hip roll unresolved: 0.2° torso response, too small to read). That 3° in the roll chain is 3–6× the 0.5–1.0° backlash the sim trains against, and it sits in exactly the axis that rocks. Also measured: the stance is asymmetric — weight on the right foot (right-leg joints move the torso more than the rigid sim, left-leg joints less: L ankle +4° → 0.2° vs 2.4° sim), and the right ankle at only −2° tipped the whole robot 8.5° (tilt guard, homed cleanly) — under 2° of pitch margin on the loaded foot. Knees not swept. Ops notes for the next bench script: the serial CLI drops about half of all lines at any spacing (wait for the reply pattern and resend); two 30 fps webcams plus the serial bridge on one USB hub re-enumerated three times tonight — one 640×480 camera alone was fine; and one RESET SERVOS over the link reported success but moved nothing (positions verified by scan; the verdict means "written", not "moved" — homeAll wants a position readback). Data: hw_sessions/2026-09-02/play_sweep4.csv, play_compare.txt, sim_ref/sim_sweep.txt.

v27full is born, and it is healthy — the first policy raised entirely inside the measured servo. Night 1 of the from-scratch synthesis (v25full recipe + act-lag 2–12 Hz + speed-clock ×1.25 from step zero) reached 59M steps before the 07:00 hard stop, reward −75 → 713 peak / 640 at the cut — and at the 35M mark it sits at 536 vs the v25full benchmark's 507 at the same age: carrying the lag contract costs nothing in growth rate. Its column signature proves the adaptation: 0/144 with 126 W of thrash on the lag-less plant, 16/144 at a calm 3.3 W in its own lagged world (falls 79%, rhythm 60%/CV 0.58 — the usual infancy, v25full looked the same at this age; judge by curve, reel is an infant reel). From here the lag column is the only honest CPU judge for the v27 era. v27full_b continues tonight, same contract. Second result: the 24-round re-distill worked — v27tilt_b_s128r24 = 41/144 under measured lag (12-round student 28, teacher 46; stand_off 8/8, push_gauntlet 4/8), so DAgger depth was the distillation bottleneck and the chained lag-referee CMD job pattern held. That student is now the best deployable candidate we own — 2.2× the flashed v26lag_s128's 19 — pending the real-robot A/B (kanban t_856978e0), which the hardware thread's evening finding makes more interesting: their roll-limit-cycle work says ~3° of passive hip-roll PLAY — free hysteresis, a third plant term nothing in sim models yet — is what actually topples real stands; their measure-then-model plan is the right order, and once the twin rocks like the robot the fleet re-ranks again. Housekeeping: fixed the eval_precision speed_mae KeyError that fall-heavy infants trigger (it's why the collect gave v27full only a SIL card).

update · 2026·09·02 · training thread

The referee got the measured servo — and the fleet ranking inverted. Following the morning card's finding (below), the CPU referee now has the missing actuation dynamics: walker_env gained act_lag_hz (the same 3-stage cascade law env_mjx trains against, seeded and ordered identically — parity pinned by tests/test_act_lag_referee.py), and eval_precision --act-lag-hz 2.0 writes a new scorecard_lag column at the bench-measured pole, leaving every historical column untouched (9cecd71). Re-refereeing the fleet against the servo we actually own (lag-less CPU → lag): v27tilt_b 46 → 46/144 — the only policy whose score does not move, 4/18 scenarios clean, asym 10%; the flashed v26lag_s128 84 → 19; the sim champion v25full_c 96 → 16 with 77% falls (the lag-naive from-scratch line is the most fragile of all — exactly why tonight's v27full carries act-lag from birth); v26lag 95 → 15; v26servo 10 → 14 (15% falls, 3.1 W, wobble 0.21 — the calmest policy in the fleet, but gait asym 81%: stable and barely locomoting, "specialized" confirmed). So this morning's "tilt generation regressed" verdict — mine — was the third casualty of the lag-less columns in two days: judged against the measured servo, v27tilt_b is the best policy we have, by 2.4×. Its s128 student keeps only part of that: 28/144 under lag (43% falls, stand_off 7/8) — still ahead of the flashed 19, but distillation is now the bottleneck (this student's val MAE 0.031 vs 0.022 for the cleanest prior distill), so a 24-round re-distill with a CHAINED lag referee is queued ahead of tonight's main run. Two honest caveats. (1) The 2.0 Hz / 3-stage pin comes from one bench session; the real robot walked on 09·01 while this column scores the flashed policy 19/144 — referee scenarios are far harder than a walk-day stand-and-stride, so treat the column as a RANKING, not a prediction, until a real A/B (v27tilt_b_s128 vs v26lag_s128 on the robot) calibrates it. (2) Rhythm under lag is bad everywhere (v26lag 96%/CV 0.16 → 64%/0.30; v27tilt_b 56%/0.49) — natural movement at the measured pole is still unsolved; that is now the era's problem statement. Also closed: the "distill self-referee dies after save" mystery — nothing crashes; distill_student.py simply ends at "saved →" and no distill job ever chained a referee step (future distill CMD jobs get && eval_precision --sil). Tonight: 38 = v27full retry (its 2-minute 09·01 death is still unexplained; exact flag set is smoke-testing on CPU) with 39 = v25full_d as the dead-birth backup.

update · 2026·09·02 · hardware thread

v27tilt_b: 46/144. The referee can't see the servo lag — and tilt-trained policies learned to hide inside it. Yesterday's card named the world-z/gravity observability bug as the cause of v27tilt's 54/144. That bug was real and the fix (ff320ae) verified, but it was not the cause: loco_v27tilt_b (v26lag's exact recipe + corrected tilt, 60.6 M steps, 7.5 h, PPO eval 1112→1336 peak, 1200 final — the best MJX curve in the lineage) refereed 46/144 with the identical signature: 122 W to stand still, 34 % falls, heading/goal 0/8. So I ran the policies in their own MJX env with a stand command (flat, no pushes, no fallen starts — sim/mjx/stand_probe.py): v27tilt_b stands at 11.9 W flat and 11.0 W at 3° tilt, zero falls in 6 seeds — indistinguishable from v26lag (11.7 W). The 122 W exists only in the CPU referee — and survives --nominal (112 W with every DR/noise/latency/backlash term off; v26lag 13.6 W). Same torso_up sensor in both engines, so not a convention flip. The discriminator: act-lag OFF in MJX reproduces the referee — v27tilt_b 11.9 → 96.4 W, v26lag 11.7 → 16.1 W. The tilt-trained policy learned a control law that is smooth only through the 2–12 Hz lag cascade it trained with (fast, large target swings the filter turns into motion); the CPU referee has no actuation lag at all (walker_env — none), so it sees the raw swings. Students: the deployed v26lag_s128 is calm both ways (10.7 / 12.5 W); v27tilt_b_s128 is 10.5 W with lag and 62.9 W, 67 % falls without — more fragile than its teacher. No flash; v26lag_s128 stays. Two conclusions. (1) The referee is now judging policies for a servo we measured does not exist: the STS3215 has ~1.7 Hz tracking bandwidth (tools/servo_frf.py), the CPU referee actuates instantly. Every act-lag policy (v26lag, v26servo, v27*) is scored against the wrong plant — v26servo's 10/144 (09·01 card) is the same story. The referee needs the measured servo dynamics (act-lag, or the servo-profile model on the agent branch) before it can rank another lag-trained run; this is the "make the sim match reality" item, and it is on the referee side. (2) Tilt itself is not yet judged: the referee has no floor tilt either, and in MJX v26lag already stands 0/6 falls at 3°, so the desk lean may not be why the real robot topples. Also today: the distill self-referee died after "saved" again (third time); v27tilt_b_s128 was probed, not refereed.

update · 2026·09·01 · hardware thread

Floor-tilt DR, first cut, was a push in disguise — and the squat has never been paid for. Walk day on the hard-rubber mat: v26lag_s128 stood ~9 s and survived a stride (vs <2 s the day before), then toppled slowly during plain stand — both attempts, on a desk the bubble level says leans ~3.5°. The firmware fall⇒disarm fired cleanly on the sidestep fall. Tom's call: randomize the floor angle ±3° in training. Implemented as a per-env gravity tilt (--tilt-max 3, 80ce2a7), which crashed at launch twice (float() under jit, then a tracer leak from the lazily built DR cache — d51400e). loco_v27tilt then trained clean: 60.6 M steps, 7.2 h, PPO reward 1112→1176 — and refereed 54/144 against v26lag's 95, with 115 W spent standing still (v26lag: 6.9 W) and every heading/goal scenario collapsed (turn_180 8→2, circle 8→1, goal_home 8→2). Root cause, verified in code: the tilt rotated opt.gravity, but the IMU up-vector (framezaxis), the upright/fall up_z and both CoM-over-foot kernels measure against world z. The policy trained against a constant unobservable lateral pull while being paid to stay world-vertical — a push, not a floor — and learned to brace. A real IMU reads gravity. Fixed (ff320ae): gravity-aligned frame from the per-env model applied to obs, up_z and the CoM projections, gated so every tilt-off recipe stays bit-identical; verified on v5body (world-vertical robot reads 3.00° under 3° tilt, gravity-plumb robot reads 0.02°, CoM shifts the expected 13.1 mm). loco_v27tilt_b is tonight's run: v26lag's exact recipe + corrected tilt, a one-variable A/B against 95/144. Separately, why squat_reps is 0/8 for every policy: both v26lag and v27tilt show depth_err 9.7 cm with zero falls — the robot never leaves standing height. The referee doubling the crouch command share (6→12 %) changed nothing because cmd_moving ignores the crouch channel: a commanded crouch is a plain stand, so w_still (joint velocity) and w_stand_com (2 cm CoM kernel) penalize the descent while w_height pays 0.03/step for tracking it. Ignoring the command is the rational policy — and matches what the real robot did when told to crouch. v28 needs a height-tracking kernel weighted like alive and a w_still gate that releases during the crouch transition; that is a reward fix, not more samples.

update · 2026·09·01

The act-lag experiment repeated our 08·27 negative — and points at v27. The hardware thread's excellent servo work (measured: the STS3215 has a ~10 rad/s² acceleration cap — THE sim-real gap, real joints move at ~half sim speed) produced --act-lag DR and an overnight run, v26servo (act-lag 2–12 Hz, warm from v22fix_e). It refereed at 10/144 with 26% falls and 81 W — failed under its own trained conditions. Same mechanism as 08·27: act-lag changes actuation dynamics — an obs-dynamics contract change that cannot be warm-started, doubly so onto a decayed-lineage policy. Kanban card filed advising against flashing its s128 student. The evidence from both threads composes into one move: loco_v27full, from scratch, the proven v25full recipe plus act-lag 2–12 Hz from step zero — a policy born expecting the real servo's sluggishness. Queued tonight behind the twice-bumped v22fix_b_s128 distill (still the best near-term hardware stopgap, projected ~80 vs the flashed 69). v25full (96/144, curve still climbing) pauses but stays the sim benchmark; if v27full tracks its growth curve while carrying act-lag, it becomes the deploy line and v25full retires to reference. Note: the SIL clock gate was corrected again (8002802) — SIL numbers from before 08·31 need re-refereeing before deploy comparisons.

update · 2026·08·29

The entropy experiment settled it: warm-starting is done. Tom's (fair) challenge to yesterday's from-scratch call produced a split A/B: continue the best warm line with entropy raised 0.004 → 0.010 (if the decay was entropy collapse, this should revive it) vs. the first 35M of the from-scratch consolidation. update · 2026·08·28

The lineages are exhausted — breaking the continuation loop. Last night's repair arms both declined again: the clock lineage's pure continuation (identical contract) collapsed its own crown jewel (rhythm CV 0.09 → 0.36, alternation 86%), and doubling the schedule weight didn't arrest the fix-line's slide (CV 0.19, 82/144). Across the last four arms the picture is uniform: training reward at all-time highs (1680–1748) while every behavioral metric degrades. That's not bad luck — it's the signature of deep- continuation decay: both lines are now 5–6 generations of warm-starts deep, the policies have gone exploitative and brittle, and further nights on these weights buy reward, not behavior. Tonight breaks the loop: loco_v25full, trained FROM SCRATCH with the full consolidated contract — every proven shaping term plus the speed-coupled clock at the servo-feasible ×1.25 baked in from step zero (the mid-lineage cap change that failed on 08·27 gets its fair test the right way). One job, the whole night (70M budgeted, curfew checkpoints), continuation tomorrow if the curve says so. Meanwhile the hardware-validation candidates are frozen: v22fix_c for scenario breadth (94/144), and v24clockv for gait quality (100% alternation, CV 0.09, slow metronome solved) — both reels and weights ready whenever the robot is.

update · 2026·08·27

Negative result, worth its price: don't change the clock contract under a trained policy. Both ×1.25 arms regressed on every axis — 62 and 63/144, stand_off back to 0/8, turn_180 0/8, and the rhythm broke too (88% alternation, stride CV 0.23/0.33). Tellingly, training reward rose (1600–1800, the highest yet) while every measured skill fell: with the clock's speed-law changed underfoot, PPO re-optimized into a different optimum and forgot the scenario skills. Contrast with history: reward-weight changes (adding the schedule, heading 0.3, stand-com) have always warm-started cleanly. It's the observation-dynamics contract that must stay fixed within a lineage. The ×1.25 idea isn't dead — it would need training from scratch or a multi-night transition budget — but it's shelved. Tonight returns to the two proven parents, each with a contract-safe fix: v24clockv_b continues the rhythm-champion clock lineage at its native ×1.7 (its top end is servo-capped anyway; betting time recovers scenarios like it did for the v22fix line), and v22fix_d continues the scenario champion with the contact-schedule weight doubled to 1.0 to arrest its three-night rhythm slide (CV 0.06 → 0.20).

update · 2026·08·26

The speed-clock A/B split — and exposed a quiet decay in the "winning" line. By scorecard the plain control won again: v22fix_c posted 94/144 (10 clean), first-ever reversal passes (2/8), top speed 0.41 m/s. The speed-clock arm (v24clockv, 87/144) fixed exactly what it was built for — the slow metronome rung went from 30% cadence error to 2% — but lost the top end (top_speed 0.25): the ×1.7 cap demands 2.55 Hz stepping, which needs ~4.4 rad/s hip swings, over the measured 4.04 rad/s STS3215 ceiling. The cap was asking for physically impossible cadence. But the rhythm probes flip the verdict: v24clockv walks at 100% alternation, stride CV 0.09, while the plain line has eroded three nights straight — CV 0.06 → 0.12 → 0.20, alternation 94% — buying scenario passes by drifting back toward the surge-stall gait we cured. For a natural walker the clock architecture is right; the cap was wrong. Tonight, both arms at a feasible ×1.25 (~1.9 Hz max, inside the servo envelope): v24clock_b continues the clock lineage; v24clock_x grafts the clock onto the scenario-stronger v22fix_c. Lineage race decides who carries forward.

update · 2026·08·25

Best card yet (84/144) — and the next wall has a name: the clock caps the speed. The knee-bias A/B resolved in the most instructive way possible: BOTH arms fixed the passive stand. v23knee (the +0.10 rad bias) went stand_off 7/8 with 0% falls overall, proving the physics probe right — but the plain control v22fix_b went stand_off 8/8 on its own (the stand-com kernel just needed a second night to consolidate a passively stable pose) and recovered turn_180 to 7/8 (hErr 8°, was 25–30° everywhere else), posting 84/144 — the best overall card to date. Third data point of the same lesson: give the recipe training time before adding terms. v22fix_b is the line; the knee-bias knob stays on the shelf, validated, in case the sag returns. Rhythm on both: 98–99% alternation, CV 0.12–0.14 (soft watch item — was 0.06). What's left all shares one root cause: top speed is pinned at 0.37 m/s ≈ 1.5 Hz × 25 cm strides. speed_ladder (top_speed 0.37 vs 1.0 commanded), reversal (t_reverse 0.53 s — fast! — but never reaches the go-speed), and the metronome's slow rung (cadence_err 30% at 1.0 Hz vs 2% elsewhere) are all the policy locked to one cadence by the very schedule reward that cured the limp. Fix built today: a speed-coupled gait clock — cadence scales with the commanded planar speed (sqrt law, ×1.0 at 0.35 m/s, clipped [0.7, 1.7]), one deterministic contract mirrored in the training env and the referee (parity-tested), firmware threading to follow before deploy, exactly the clock-freeze path. Tonight: v24clockv (speed-clock on, warm from v22fix_b) vs v22fix_c (plain control).

update · 2026·08·24

v22fix is the new line — and the passive stand has a second, subtler failure. The 08·19 A/B: v22fix (heading 0.3 + stand-com 1.0) kept the metronome perfectly (100% alternation, stride CV 0.06 — heading at 0.3 is rhythm-safe where 1.0 wasn't) and the stand-com kernel did exactly its job: standing CoM went from 28 mm aft to 1–6 mm. Falls 4%, square/goal-home 8/8. The plain control (v21sched_c) meanwhile decayed — rhythm slipped to 95%/CV 0.20 and the card fell to 58/144, so the shaping terms aren't just scaffolding, they hold the behavior up. But stand_off only reached 3/8: with the CoM centered, the per-joint probe shows the remaining failure is a slow sag-collapse — knees and ankles fold together ~1.3°/s from a dead-straight leg. A pure-physics sweep from v22fix's own stand pose found the fix: a +0.10 rad knee bias flips the release from a 28 cm collapse to a 5 cm hold (the opposite bias falls backward). That's now --w-stand-knee; tonight: v23knee (+knee bias) vs v22fix_b (plain control, also watching whether turn_180 — currently under-rotating by 25° with zero falls in both arms — recovers with time). Note for the hardware session: stand_off passivity rests on the 0.35 Nm backdrive-friction estimate — it's the cheapest, safest scenario to validate sim-vs-real first.

update · 2026·08·19

A/B verdict: keep the rhythm, drop the heading kernel at 1.0. The plain continuation (v21sched_b, +35M) kept the metronomic gait (100% alternation, stride CV 0.06) and re-learned steering inside it — line 6/8, backward 7/8, turn 5/8, square 7/8, goal-home 7/8. The heading arm (v21head) recovered station-keeping brilliantly (stand_off 7/8, falls 1%, 8 scenarios clean) but paid with the crown jewel: alternation fell to 88%, stride CV back to 0.33 — at weight 1.0 the integrated-heading kernel pushes the policy back into off-schedule correction steps. v21sched_b is the line going forward. Remaining sore spots on the b-arm: stand_off falls 8/8 and metronome — which now tracks tempo (cadErr 2%, was the original failure) and fails only on wobble during changes. Both reels confirm the full-footprint foot collision fix: standing feet stay separated. stand_off diagnosed same day: the pose-at-cut probe shows the v21 line parks its standing CoM 26–28 mm aft of the midfoot point; with torque released the ankle gravity moment (~0.60 Nm) beats the servo backdrive friction (~0.35 Nm ≈ 16 mm of offset) and it topples backward at ~6.5 s — policies standing at ≤18 mm survive, including v21head. Nothing in the recipe shaped the double-support stand CoM (w_com_stance is single-support only), so a stand-gated CoM-over-midfoot kernel (--w-stand-com) now exists. Tonight: v22fix (heading 0.3 + stand-com 1.0 — disjoint gates, so scenario attribution stays clean) vs v21sched_c (plain control).

update · 2026·08·18

Cadence fixed — the limp is gone. Cost: steering. The contact-schedule reward, one night in (loco_v21sched): cadence goes metronomic — 100% step alternation, stride period 637 ± 39 ms (CV 0.06 vs 0.21–0.30 before), step length 20 ± 3 cm (was 12 ± 6).

The rhythm result cost lane keeping — line/backward pass rates fell to 2/8 and 0/8 purely on lateral drift (0.21 m vs the 0.15 limit) and heading (18°), with zero falls: the policy used to steer with off-schedule correction steps and hasn't relearned steering inside the new rhythm in 45M steps. Tonight's A/B, both warm from v21sched: plain continuation vs --w-heading 1.0 (integrated-heading kernel). stand_off is also still regressed (1/8) — the deploy candidate remains v19feet_b until this line recovers.

update · 2026·08·17

Verdict (Tom): the forward walk still looks like limping — confirmed, but it isn't left/right. Per-leg probe at 0.35 m/s: step counts, lengths, and swing times now match across sides (83/83 steps, 12.1 cm both legs, no per-seed side bias). What's wrong is the rhythm: step length 12 ± 6 cm, touchdown phase 0.53 ± 0.27 of the stride cycle, and long steps arrive in bursts (lag-1 autocorr up to +0.57) — a surge-stall-surge cadence that reads as a limp. Same root cause as metronome 0/8 and speed mae 0.30: the policy ignores its own gait clock. Next lever: a contact-schedule reward (feet paid for touching down on the clock's phase), then AMP motion priors.

update · 2026·08·15

Left/right symmetry fixed — but the walk still isn't smooth (see the 08·17 verdict above). And the feet stopped ghosting through each other. Two structural fixes landed overnight. First, the plant had no left-foot/right-foot collision: on turns and sidesteps the soles interpenetrated on ~half of all steps, up to 46 mm deep. Explicit sole/shank contact pairs plus a retrain (loco_v19feet_b) closed the hole — the same probe now measures ≤2% shallow-contact steps. Second, loco_v20mirror added a mirror-symmetry loss on the policy itself (penalize π(mirror(obs)) ≠ mirror(π(obs)), the signed permutation derived from the plant and pinned by physics tests): gait asymmetry fell 31% → 12% — a number the per-touchdown swing penalty hadn't moved in 110M+ steps — with power down 17.6 → 14.0 W and 6/18 scenarios fully clean (best yet).

The run was cut at the 07:00 curfew (50.8M of 70M steps), so the mirror loss hasn't converged — sym_loss was still falling (0.010 → 0.008).

update · 2026·08·12

The v5body era: new pelvis, honest joint limits, and a 90-hour marathon. The robot got its as-built body (pelvis v6, camera CG corrected by 68 mm, every servo's measured 2026-08-02 range finally applied — knees ±95°), and the referee grew a responsiveness suite: command-reversal latency, metronome cadence, squats, weight shifts. Best policy so far is loco_v18b_mix: 78/144 scenario seeds, 11% falls, goal-home to 5 cm, first-ever turn-180 passes, and a 0.5 s reversal response.

2026·08·14, the frozen-gait-clock runs (v18e/v18f): stillness kept (0.9 W, wobble 0.08 rad/s, torque-off stand 7/8) AND the cost of calm repaid — turn-180 8/8 at 4° heading error, sidesteps and rough ground 8/8. The recipe is now trading scenarios against each other instead of accumulating (returns/reversal dipped as turning recovered; overall flat at ~77/144), so the next lever is structural: mirror-symmetry augmentation, then AMP motion priors. Full story below is the July log.

It walks. Ten seconds, and it can be told what to do.

Five days of CPU training could sprint but never walk — no policy survived 10 s, and day 5 proved the missing ingredient was scale. Tonight's first GPU run (150M steps in 2h18m on a desk-side RTX 4070 Ti) produced one policy that walks, turns, pivots, and stands on command — with the GoPro mounted, 0–8 ms latency, gear backlash, and IMU-only sensing, verified in the CPU engine it wasn't trained in.

01 The wall came down at scale

The day-5 diagnosis said sustained walking was a training-scale problem, not a reward problem. Tested tonight: the same reward family and the same plant, ported to MJX (JAX) and trained with brax PPO at 2048 parallel robots on Mira's RTX 4070 Ti — 150M steps in 2h18m, versus ~8M overnight on the CPU rig. Hard mode from step zero: realizable IMU-only observations, 0–8 ms latency, 0.5–1° backlash, servo-gain error, random shoves, GoPro payload. Mean episode length rose 36 → 465/500 with no curriculum and no warm start.

Trust rule: MJX numbers are never the claim. The port is parity-tested against the CPU engine (per-step physics exact to 1e-11; one documented contact-manifold difference at impact transients), and every policy is re-evaluated by the CPU referee — the engine every previous result lived in — under the conditions of the claim. 8 seeds per scenario, 10 s episodes:

CommandSurvive 10 sSpeed errWobble RMSServo draw
walk 0.6 m/s7/80.12 m/s0.73 rad/s · calm19.4 W
walk 0.35 m/s8/80.06 m/s0.5814.5 W
stand8/80.01 m/s0.065.2 W
pivot left / right16/16—0.082–7 W
walking turn 0.4 + 0.4 rad/s8/80.09 m/s0.6615.5 W

One policy does all of it — the per-skill expert + distillation plan is retired. Soft spots, named: one walk seed in eight falls; heading wanders during straight walks (loose yaw-rate tracking, next reward iteration); pivot turn-rate authority still to be quantified. Full details in DESIGN.md §Stage 2b.

02 It sits up — and that's a design finding

New scenario: get up after a fall. Trained from 2048 settled ragdoll falls (no fall termination; reward = height + uprightness progress + a standing bonus). The run was stopped at 100M steps by a pre-agreed rule: reward had plateaued for 30M+ steps while the standing metric never left zero. The policy's answer, verified by the CPU referee (0/8 recoveries): from any fall it reorganizes into a stable sit in about a second — then waits, motionless, at 0.9 W.

The follow-up study made it precise — and found a bug that had handicapped every policy ever trained: the action mapping couldn't reach the deep half of the knee's range (capped at −50° of −95°). With that fixed and the joint-limit question answered by static path analysis (a balanced sit→stand exists at ≥95° of hip flexion, provably not at ≤90° — the current yoke stops at 60°), a retrain at 110° moved the ceiling:

The remaining gap is the last 14 cm: the pike from kneel/squat to standing traverses a ±20 mm balance corridor on a 90 mm foot. Probes cleared the physics suspects (peak torque 1.08 of 2.72 N·m available; failure identical at 1–4× floor friction) — it's a closed-loop balance problem, plus a corridor that bigger sole pads would widen directly. Decision pending: yoke redesign to −110°/+60° (the 95° bound stands regardless) + larger feet + one more training round, or ship v1 with manual reset after falls.

03 The reckoning: the old gait was unbuildable

Until now the sim's actuators were idealized position servos — infinitely strong. Day three replaced them with the real thing: PD control clamped to the STS3215's torque–speed envelope (2.94 N·m stall tapering to zero at no-load speed, scaled by supply voltage; parameters fitted to a servo-like step response, then randomized in training). Verdict on the old champion: terrain_v4 demanded ~3 N·m at 4.4 rad/s — outside the motor's envelope at any voltage. Dropped onto honest actuators it collapses within 1.5 s. Warm-starting couldn't fix it (same lesson as the shuffle); training from scratch inside the envelope could.

04 The battery verdict: 2S works, 3S wins — 3S it is

Same dash task, two supply voltages (16 episodes each; a finish = crossing 2 m and standing upright 1 s later):

PolicyVFlatMedian dash+GoPro 154 g10 mm bumpsGoPro + bumpsModel-error DR
dash_11v1_hard11.1 16/162.72 s 16/1616/16 16/1616/16
dash_7v4_hard7.4 16/164.36 s 15/1616/16 12/1616/16

Decision made 07·11: 3S. The tower was reworked around it — a 3S 850 mAh pack (~80 g, XT30) now tilt-loads through a window in the rear wall for tool-free swaps (peel the belt, tug the ribbon; the fly-in animation below shows the pack passing through the window). Torso inertia was rebuilt for the lighter pack and the dash policies re-verified on it: 16/16, median 2.67 s with the GoPro on. 2S remains a tested fallback at every level.

05 The camera rides on top

A GoPro MAX (154 g) now mounts on a printable three-prong base atop the tower — a bolt-on crash fuse that shears before the tower does. The driver board moved inside; total 1043 g, CG +29 mm. The policy trains with the payload randomized 0–170 g, so one policy handles camera-on and camera-off.

  • Slots 3.2 mm — test-fit the MAX's fingers before printing everything.
  • All 30 joint-sweep interference checks still pass.

06 How it got here

  1. A Gymnasium env around the MuJoCo model

    36-dim observation, actions as residual target angles around the standing pose. Reward: forward velocity + upright + alive − energy − jitter.

    day 1 · walker_env.py

  2. Baseline PPO found the cheat, not the gait

    Uncapped forward reward → a 1.3 m faceplant dive. Fixed by capping rewarded speed so a steady gait out-earns a lunge; domain randomization then hardened the walk against ±15% model error.

    day 1 · shaped_v2 → v6

  3. The shuffle became a stride

    Feet-air-time + single-support shaping restructured the gait (speed rose 0.53→0.79 m/s with the cap unchanged), and a per-episode procedural heightfield made it hold up on ±15 mm rough ground.

    day 2 · gait_v6 → terrain_v4

  4. Honest muscles, real body, a stopwatch

    CAD-true masses and mesh-derived inertia, the STS3215 torque–speed envelope, the GoPro payload, and the timed 2 m dash — the policies above.

    day 3 · dash_11v1_hard / dash_7v4_hard

  5. Real senses, commands, and an honest reckoning

    The robot lost every sensor it doesn't own (IMU-only observations), gained a command interface (velocity + yaw rate, zero = stand), survived an external review (pad-true feet, backlash, power metering) — and then a reframe landed: dash episodes end 1 s past the line, so no policy had ever practiced walking 10 s. Eight CPU runs failed to fix it; the write-up called scale the binding constraint.

    day 4–5 · imu_hard / cmd_11v2 / the wall

  6. MJX at 2048 robots: the wall comes down

    The env ported to JAX (parity 1e-11 vs the CPU engine), brax PPO on the RTX 4070 Ti, 150M hardened steps in 2h18m — and the first policy that walks, turns, pivots, and stands on command, confirmed by the CPU referee. Scale was the whole story.

    day 5 night · sim/mjx · mjx_cmd_v1

07 Open items

  • Control latency — the day-3 top risk. Closed: the 0/16 collapse was an artifact of a doubled whole-step delay; with sub-step modeling, realistic 2–5 ms latency barely registers. Latency-DR fine-tunes (dash_11v1_hardlat3: 28/32, median 2.72 s at 4 ms + GoPro; dash_7v4_hardlat: 32/32, 4.50 s) push the cliff to ~10–14 ms — beyond that it's a firmware call (run the loop on the ESP32), not a training problem. Details in DESIGN.md §sub-step latency.
  • 2S or 3S — the battery-bay decision above. Decided: 3S, bay reworked for tool-free swap, order unblocked.
  • Overnight (day 4): the robot got its real sensor suite in sim. dash_11v1_imu_hard runs on encoders + a noisy BNO085 IMU only (no torso velocity/height — nothing measures them): 16/16 @ 2.28 s flat, 15/16 on terrain and at 6 ms latency, but 8–9/16 with the GoPro fixed at 154 g — the realizable policy's one weak column. Fix candidates: an on-ESP32 velocity estimator fed as an observation, or payload-focused training.
  • Stop-and-stand is an open problem. Solved — by changing the question. Three dash_stop attempts each found a new reward exploit (all documented in DESIGN.md); the fix was retiring the finish-line structure for command-conditioned locomotion (track a commanded velocity + yaw rate, where zero = stand). The command policy stands on command 8/8 with ~4 cm drift, from any start, even hardened with GoPro + latency. It also gives first turning capability: pivots track both directions (≈0.2 rad/s left / 0.1 right — the identical-parts gait turns left for free), walking turns left-only so far.
  • Day-5 evening reframe: NO policy has ever walked 10 s. Resolved the same night — the scale hypothesis was correct. mjx_cmd_v1 (150M GPU steps) walks the full 10 s and passes all six command scenarios in the CPU referee (section 01). Bigger feet are now optional insurance rather than a blocker; the 2 m dash remains the snappiest hardware demo.
  • Command-mode walking hit an honest wall (day 5). Resolved by scale; the distillation plan is retired — one GPU-trained policy handles the whole command family. The day's metrics stack (wobble RMS, electrical watts) carried forward and referees every new policy. New soft spots to work: 1/8 walk-seed fall, wandering heading on straight walks (yaw kernel or heading term), pivot turn-rate authority unquantified.
  • The 11.1 V gait still jogs (flight phase); the grounded 7.4 V gait is the more sim-to-real-plausible first candidate.
  • Repeated shoves remain unsolved (unchanged from day 1).
